prompt: Suppose $A\leq_p B$ via a polynomial-time many-one reduction. Which consequence is guaranteed?

answers.explanation: To decide A, transform its input into an equivalent B-instance in polynomial time, then run the polynomial-time decider for B.

answers.text: $A$ and $B$ must be the same language.
answers.explanation: A reduction can map between different languages.
Reducibility alone says nothing of that sort.
A reduction imposes no such requirement.
An easy problem can reduce to a harder one; the implication goes the other way.
Reducing an NP problem to B does not give a verifier for all of B.
A reduction from an arbitrary A does not establish NP-hardness or membership in NP.

answers.text: If $B$ is NP-hard, then $A$ is NP-hard.
answers.explanation: Hardness transfers from the source to the target, not generally from the target to the source.
A can be easy even when B is hard.

answers.text: The reduction must be invertible in polynomial time.
answers.explanation: Many-one reductions need preserve the yes/no answer, not be invertible.
